conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Carter, a perinatal mental-health specialist. My job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived, and to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

We’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a 10-question screen that looks at mood, anxiety, and coping over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise, or if we ever need to talk about keeping you safe. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification whenever you need.

Ready to begin?

**Question 1**  
Thinking back over the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Most days I’ve been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before I was pregnant, but when my partner makes a silly joke or when the baby does a funny little face, I still catch myself giggling.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I’d say most of the time I can still laugh—maybe a little less than before, but definitely more days than not.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I’ve still looked forward to things—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over to help with the baby. They’re small things, but I do enjoy them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up a ton or won’t settle, I might think “maybe I ate something that bothered him” or “did I wait too long to swaddle?”—but it’s just a quick thought, not something I beat myself up over.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing sounds different or that I didn’t sanitize the bottles well enough, even when everything looks fine. It’s not constant—just little waves of worry that pop up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that kind of sudden panic. A couple of times my heart races when I’m trying to swaddle him fast and he’s crying, but it’s more “hurry up” than actual fear.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then, yeah—like yesterday when the laundry pile looked like a mountain and the baby wanted to nurse again right after I’d finally sat down. It felt a bit much for a minute, but I took a breath, asked my partner to hold her, and the feeling passed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened. Once the baby’s down for the night I usually drift off pretty easily—if anything, it’s her wake-ups that disturb my sleep, not my mood.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve had a couple of weepy moments—like when I couldn’t get her to latch at 3 a.m.—but it’s not an all-day sad feeling. It comes and goes quickly, and most of the day I feel okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve cried maybe twice this week—once when she wouldn’t nap and I was really tired—but it was just for a minute, and then I felt fine again.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. I would never want to hurt myself—I just want to be here for my baby and get through these early weeks the best I can.

You've shared that early motherhood is mostly manageable with moments of laughter and enjoyment, though you do notice occasional <sym>worry waves</sym> about your baby's safety and brief <sym>tearfulness</sym> when tired. You can still ask for help, look forward to small pleasures, and you have no thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 7, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes specific, recurrent worries about baby care that arise without clear triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to 1(Q1)+0(Q2)+1(Q3)+2(Q4)+0(Q5)+1(Q6)+0(Q7)+1(Q8)+1(Q9)+0(Q10)=7. A score <8 suggests <med>postpartum depression</med> is unlikely per validated cut-offs. While you endorsed <sym>anxiety</sym> "sometimes" (Q4) and mild <sym>overwhelm</sym> (Q6), you denied persistent low mood, guilt, panic, sleep disturbance from mood, and self-harm. These findings do not meet threshold for <med>DSM-5 Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which requires ≥5 symptoms including depressed mood or loss of interest most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥2 weeks. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue enjoying your support system; share feelings with partner and visiting family
2. Practice brief self-care (5-minute shower, stroller walk) when baby naps to buffer stress
3. Re-screen with EPDS at 6-week postpartum visit or sooner if symptoms worsen or persist
4. If <sym>worry</sym> becomes intrusive or daily function declines, contact your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> for further evaluation
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wks post-delivery, exclusively breastfeeding, partner and maternal support present.

Self-report on EPDS-10 items:

Symptoms endorsed  
• Transient tearfulness (twice this week)  
• Momentary “waves” of unprovoked worry about infant safety  
• Occasional feeling of being overwhelmed; resolves with brief support

Symptoms denied  
• Persistent low mood, sustained anhedonia  
• Excessive self-blame or guilt  
• Panic spells, nocturnal mood-related insomnia  
• Self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Overall affective stability; able to enjoy daily activities, use coping strategies, and mobilize help. No safety concerns identified.

Screening significance  
Current score approximates 4–5 (below standard cut-off ≥10 for depression; ≥6 for anxiety). Findings suggest mild, situational distress rather than clinically significant postpartum depression or anxiety disorder.

Recommendation  
Continue routine postpartum follow-up; re-screen if symptoms worsen, persist >2 weeks, or functional impairment emerges.
